title: Concurrency fanout exploration (personal lab notes)
content:
Goal:
Quick personal experiment notes to understand how different request fanout (concurrency per request) patterns affect overall latency distribution and throughput on the serving runtime. Trying to capture anomalies I saw in production traces yesterday (spiky p95 despite flat QPS).

Summary / short conclusions (TL;DR):
- Small fanout (1-2 internal workers per request) gives best p50/p95 for single-token/light prompts at low QPS.
- Medium fanout (3-8) improves throughput for long-sequence workloads by enabling parallel chunking, but increases p99 tail if network/ephemeral-connection contention exists.
- High fanout (>8) saturates socket pools and increases p95/p99 dramatically unless connection reuse + HTTP/2 multiplexing is in play.
- Warmup (pre-warming worker-side KV caches and GC) reduces tail by ~30% for medium/high fanout cases.

Environment / baseline:
- Model: open-llm/gpt-small-8k (quantized, 8-bit), sequence length in tests: 128 (short) and 2048 (long).
- Cluster: dedicated dev cluster, 4 nodes, each node: 8xA10G, 64GB RAM allocated to runtime.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime v1.14.0 (local branch with experimental fanout steering flag enabled).
- Network: same AZ, 40Gb EFA; probing used to exercise both sockets and HTTP/2 multiplexing toggles.
- Client driver: synthetic runner (python, async), simulating N concurrent incoming requests at target QPS. Each request fanout means the request is split into F internal parallel shards/workers and merged.
- Metrics captured: request latency histogram (p50/p90/p95/p99), CPU utilization, node-level network RX/TX, open sockets count, connection pool stats, internal queue lengths, KV-cache hit rate.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Vary fanout F = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]
- Two prompt types: short (128 tokens), long (2048 tokens)
- QPS targets: low (50), medium (250), high (1000) total incoming requests
- Warmup toggle: cold (no warm KV), warmed (run 10x warmup set)
- Connection mode: http1 (pool), http2 (multiplex), persistent sockets vs ephemeral

Representative raw results (short prompt):
Case: short prompt, QPS=250, warm=false- F=1: p50=48ms, p95=130ms, p99=240ms, throughput=248rps- F=2: p50=55ms, p95=150ms, p99=270ms, throughput=255rps- F=4: p50=72ms, p95=300ms, p99=720ms, throughput=262rps- F=8: p50=88ms, p95=950ms, p99=2.4s, throughput=260rps- F=16: p50=142ms, p95=1.8s, p99=>5s (many timeouts), throughput=200rps 
Observations: at short prompt sizes, increasing fanout only adds coordination overhead and creates more network/connection contention. P99 balloons beyond F=4.

Representative raw results (long prompt):
Case: long prompt, QPS=250, warm=true- F=1: p50=240ms, p95=560ms, p99=920ms, throughput=244rps- F=2: p50=190ms, p95=430ms, p99=780ms, throughput=260rps- F=4: p50=140ms, p95=320ms, p99=540ms, throughput=280rps- F=8: p50=128ms, p95=300ms, p99=500ms, throughput=300rps- F=16: p50=130ms, p95=320ms, p99=680ms, throughput=295rps
Observations: for long sequences, moderate fanout helps by parallelizing token generation/attention compute, improving throughput and p50/p95. Past F=8 benefits plateau and p99 rises slightly due to merge overhead. Warmup helped a lot (KV cache hit rate went from 22% -> 88%).

Failure modes and anomalies seen: 
1) Socket pool exhaustion: when ephemeral connection mode used, bursts of F>4 created many simultaneous outbound connections from runtime to worker processes. OS hit ephemeral port limits on some nodes (observed TIME_WAIT spike). Reduced by switching to HTTP/2 multiplexing.
2) Queue amplification: incoming request with high F increased downstream worker queue lengths because the orchestrator sent shards faster than workers could accept, causing backpressure spikes at p95. Solution: add per-worker leaky-bucket admission (throttle shards per second).
3) Merge barrier cost: when fanout is used, the join/merge wait time becomes non-negligible, especially if worker latencies are skewed. Observed correlation between p99 and histogram of per-shard variance.
4) GC/alloc stalls: under high fanout workloads memory churn increased; tuning jemalloc arenas and lowering temporary buffer allocation reduced a 5-10% p99 tail.

Quick notes on mitigations tried: 
- HTTP/2 multiplexing: reduced socket pressure and p99 by ~25% for F>=8 (short prompt runs).
- Connection reuse + keep-alive tunings: lower connection churn.
- Adaptive fanout steering: limit F dynamically based on current open sockets and worker queue lengths. Early tests show this prevents p99 explosions at high QPS.
- Warmup batches: running small warmup traffic to pre-populate KV caches and JIT paths reduces both median and tail.
- Merge hedging: kick off 1-2 speculative re-dispatches for slow shards (experimental) — reduces p99 but increases compute cost.

Data artifacts I recorded:
- Perf CSVs: (on disk) /tmp/igor/fanout_short_qps250_warm_false.csv and fanout_long_qps250_warm_true.csv
- Traces: local jaeger traces saved to /tmp/igor/traces/ (span tags: fanout, shard_id, merge_wait_ms)
- Flamegraphs: node-level flamegraphs under /tmp/igor/flame/

Open questions / TODOs: 
- Re-run with different model sizes (medium/large) — does fanout knee shift? Hypothesis: larger models shift optimal F lower due to per-shard per-token cost.
- Evaluate cost tradeoffs: speculative hedging reduces tail but ups compute; need cost-per-request model.
- Test with real production traffic shapes (bursty multiplexing) rather than synthetic uniform QPS.
- Add per-shard deadline propagation in RPC so slow shards can be cancelled early and merge collects partial results.
- Investigate kernel tunables for TIME_WAIT mitigation (but better to fix via multiplexing).

Notes to self (practical):
- When writing up findings for the runtime team, include two clear recomendations: default fanout=1 for short prompts; default fanout=4 for long prompts but with adaptive cap that lowers F when socket/queue pressure detected.
- Talk to SRE about ephemeral port limits in the dev cluster and prod.
- Attach CSVs and traces to GH PR referenced above (redwood/inference#1824).

End of scratchpad.

-- Igor
